answer.answer: The goal was met: the study confirmed five settings on five different scenes. On 1bbe02fc, 07981e6a and 0d4893f5 the policy failed at every repeat (S19, S4, S7), and on 18f8dbd6 and 0e002edd it failed every run but with fewer repeats (S18, S10). All five are fast hand-offs (1.2x or 1.4x) with the pedestrian stepping out 0.5–1 s early. None of the triaged failures involved the pedestrian, though. The ego drifted left into a vehicle beside or ahead of it, ran into parked cars, or left the road, often while ignoring a RIGHT command. So these settings show where the 2 Hz policy breaks, not which speed–timing pairs make it hit a pedestrian. The study never ran the nominal setting (1.0x, 0 s) on these scenes, or the same speeds with other step-out times. It therefore cannot say whether the pedestrian's timing matters, or whether these scenes would fail at their recorded speed anyway. Two of the five cases are weak: S10 rests on runs flagged as possible simulator artifacts, and most of S19's road exits are marginal, with the policy's fault marked unclear.

findings.claim: On 1bbe02fc at 1.2x speed with the pedestrian 0.5 s early, every run left the road. The ego planned straight through a junction where the route turns right, and the command only switched to RIGHT at the last frame. The ego stayed within about 0.8 m of the human's path, and the policy's fault was unclear in most runs. These failures may come from tight map boundaries or late route commands rather than the speed or the timing.

On 07981e6a at 1.4x with the pedestrian 1 s early, every run failed the same way. The ego held about 12–14 m/s down a narrow street, drifted left into the parking lane and hit parked car 6, braking only slightly.

On 18f8dbd6 at 1.4x with the pedestrian 1 s early, every run failed. The ego drifted left at about 12 m/s and hit the rear of a slower car in the next lane. The same scene did not fail in single runs at 1.0x and 1.2x with the same step-out time, which hints that speed matters here. One run at each of those settings is not a rate.

On 0d4893f5 at 1.2x with the pedestrian 0.5 s early, every run failed. The ego's plan bent left and its front hit vehicle 33 in the adjacent lane, while the recorded route went straight and then right.

On 0e002edd at 1.4x with the pedestrian 1 s or 0.5 s early, every run failed. On a RIGHT command the ego turned too tight or ran straight across the junction into parked cars at the curb. Every one of these failures is flagged as a possible simulator artifact, because the ego ended more than 3.5 m from the recorded path. The triage blames the policy's steering, but this case is the least certain of the five. Single runs at 0.8x and at 1.2x on this scene did not fail.

No triaged failure in the study was a collision with the pedestrian. Every failure hit a vehicle (moving or parked) or left the road. Most share one cause: a leftward drift or a RIGHT command that the policy ignored. That pattern persists at 2 Hz planning.

18d28973 at 1.4x with the pedestrian 0.5–1 s early failed in some runs but not others, so the failure rate could lie either side of 0.5. These failures were also lane drifts into a slow white car ahead (actor 99), not pedestrian strikes.

Some settings did not fail. 0caa8f1a at 1.2x with the pedestrian 0.5 s early did not fail in five repeats. 048b974e at 1.4x with step-outs from 1.5 s to 0.5 s early did not fail in its few runs per setting. 12a09194 and 0b10bce8 got only one run each, so they are barely explored.

open: Whether these scenes fail at nominal settings: run 1.0x with no time shift on 1bbe02fc, 07981e6a, 0d4893f5, 18f8dbd6 and 0e002edd. The plan's caveat warned that several of these scenes failed at nominal settings in an earlier run with reactive traffic.

Whether the pedestrian's step-out time matters at all: repeat each confirmed speed with no shift and with 1–2 s late step-outs. All failures were collisions with vehicles or road exits, so timing may play no part.

Whether the policy ever hits the pedestrian: the failure check cannot tell which actor was hit. A pedestrian-specific contact or closest-approach measure, and runs where the step-out puts the pedestrian in the ego's path, would settle it.
Whether S19's road exits are real: check the map's road edge and the timing of the RIGHT command on 1bbe02fc, since the ego stayed within about 0.8 m of the human's path.
Whether S10 and S11 are simulator artifacts: review the videos and rendering for the 0e002edd runs flagged as more than 3.5 m off the recorded path.
18d28973 at 1.4x and -0.5 s or -1 s: more repeats are needed to tell whether the failure rate is above 0.5.
12a09194 and 0b10bce8 have one kept run each, and one 0b10bce8 run halted and was not kept. They need searching across the speed–timing grid.
Comparison with the 10 Hz study pedestrian_ego_speed: its results are not in this input. Lining up the same settings would show whether 2 Hz planning reduces the left-drift failures seen here.
